title: Answers kept apart
hook: this year each tradition answers in its own voice, and we don't blend them into one

segments.voice: Yesterday: six questions, asked inside the old texts themselves. Your line was the big six. Did one of them turn up as a real question in your day? Keep it close. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

Squeeze every tube in a child's paint box onto one plate and stir. Red, blue, yellow, green, the lovely violet. What you get is brown. Every color was beautiful on its own, and together, stirred, they cancel each other out. Wisdom from many traditions can go the same way. Take a little from here and a little from there, stir it into one soft answer, and you end up with something nobody actually holds. This year we are going to hear a great many answers. So before the first one, a rule for how we hear them.
screen: `STIR EVERY COLOR TOGETHER.` → `YOU GET BROWN.` → `A RULE BEFORE THE FIRST ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, a blended answer belongs to nobody. Take the question of suffering. The Buddha names craving as where it comes from. Job, in the ashes, argues his case before God. Stir those together into everything happens for a reason, and you've lost both of them. So this year every answer is named. The Buddha's is the Buddha's. Job's is Job's. Second, each answer comes with a life. A teaching isn't a loose sentence floating in the air. It lives inside practices, a community, a long line of people who read it and argued about it. To hear it well you have to hear where it lives. Third, alike is not the same. Some lines across traditions do sound close. Before long we'll hear the Dhammapada say that hatred ceases by love, and later in the year Jesus will say, love your enemies. Those can sit side by side as neighbors. But one belongs to the Buddha's sayings in the Dhammapada, the other to the Sermon on the Mount, and each makes the most sense in its own house. So we'll notice the echo, and leave each line at home. Fourth, swift to hear. The letter of James puts it plainly: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." And from a very different house, the Stoic Zeno is reported by the old biographer Diogenes Laertius to have said that we have two ears and one mouth so that we might listen more and talk less. Two houses, two sayings, each in its own words, and neither needs the other to make its point. Together they set this year's rule: hear the answer out before you reply to it.
screen: `A BLENDED ANSWER BELONGS TO NOBODY.` · `EACH ANSWER COMES WITH A LIFE.` · `ALIKE IS NOT THE SAME.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · then, large: `LISTEN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and listen to the room for a moment. Pick out one sound, then another, without naming them good or bad. Just hear them. Now make yourself a small promise, in your own words, for the year: that when a tradition answers one of the six questions, you'll hear it out to the end before you agree, disagree, or start mixing it with something else. You don't have to say it aloud. Just make it, and then go back to listening to the room. The bell holds the time.
Diogenes Laertius, the ancient biographer who credits Zeno with saying we have two ears and one mouth so we might listen more and talk less. Today's word.
Your line: listen first. In one conversation today, let the other person finish completely before you answer. Notice what you hear in the part you'd usually talk over. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some interfaith study groups let each tradition speak in its own texts and terms, and ask members of that tradition to explain it, rather than merging teachings into one shared answer.

fork.setup: two lines from two traditions sound almost the same: hatred ceases by love, and love your enemies. what does this year do with them?
options: decide which one says it better

trapdoor: what you thought: all the traditions are really saying the same thing.
what it means: some lines echo each other, but each answer lives in its own house, with its own practices and people.
what a scholar hears: James 1:19, and Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23, where a saying of Zeno's comes to us as a report in a biographer's book, not in Zeno's own words.
